sections.normalized_html: Some sets are so important that special symbols are used to represent them.

sections.normalized_html:
• The set [MATH: \mathbb{N}] represents the set of natural numbers. This set contains all the positive whole numbers: [MATH: \Bbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, ... \}] It's essential to remember that the natural numbers do not contain zero! However, if we wish to refer to the set of natural numbers and zero, we use the symbol [MATH: \mathbb N_0{:}] [MATH: \Bbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5,... \}]

  • The set [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] represents the set of integers. This set contains the positive and negative whole numbers and zero. [MATH: \Bbb{Z} = \left\{... , -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... \right\}] The use of the letter "Z" comes from the German word "Zahlen," which means "numbers".

  • The set [MATH: \mathbb{Q}] represents the set of rational numbers. This set contains all fractions that can be expressed as the ratio (or Quotient) of two integers.

  • The set [MATH: \mathbb{R}] represents the set of real numbers. This set contains all possible rational and irrational numbers (such as [MATH: \pi, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \ldots]).

  • The set [MATH: \mathbb C] represents the set of complex numbers. These consist of any number of the form [MATH: a+\textrm i b,] where [MATH: a,b\in\mathbb R.]

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following sets: [MATH: \mathbb N, \quad \mathbb Z, \quad \mathbb Q, \quad \mathbb R, \quad \mathbb C]

To which of these sets does the number [MATH: 3.25] belong?
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following sets:
[MATH: \mathbb N, \quad \mathbb Z, \quad \mathbb Q, \quad \mathbb R, \quad \mathbb C]

To which of these sets does the number [MATH: 3.25] belong?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall the following:

  • [MATH: \mathbb{N}] represents the set of natural numbers.

  • [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] represents the set of integers.

  • [MATH: \mathbb{Q}] represents the set of rational numbers.

  • [MATH: \mathbb{R}] represents the set of real numbers.

  • [MATH: \mathbb C] represents the set of complex numbers.

With that in mind, we note the following:

  • The number [MATH: 3.25] is not an integer, so it does not belong to [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] nor [MATH: \mathbb{N},] so we can write [MATH: 3.25\notin\mathbb N, \qquad 3.25\notin\mathbb Z.]

  • However, notice that [MATH: 3.25] can be written as the ratio of two integers as follows: [MATH: 3.25=\dfrac{325}{100}] Consequently, [MATH: 3.25] is a rational number, and we can write [MATH: 3.25 \in \mathbb{Q}.]

  • Every rational is a real and complex number. Consequently, [MATH: 3.25] belongs to both [MATH: \mathbb R] and [MATH: \mathbb{C},] and we can write [MATH: 3.25 \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad 3.25 \in \mathbb{C}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \mathbb Q, \mathbb R,] and [MATH: \mathbb C] only."

Content:
We can use subscripts and superscripts to limit the special sets to being only positive ("[MATH: +]" superscript), only negative ("[MATH: -]" superscript), and to include zero ("[MATH: 0]" subscript).

Content:
For example, [MATH: \mathbb{Z}^+] represents the positive integers, while [MATH: \mathbb{Z}^-] represents the negative integers:

[MATH: Z^{+}|= {1, 2, 3, …}; Z^{−}|= {− 1, − 2, − 3, …}]

Content:
These sets do not include [MATH: 0.] If we want to include [MATH: 0] too, then we can use a subscript [MATH: 0,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: Z_{0}^{+}|= {0, 1, 2, 3, …}; Z_{0}^{−}|= {0, − 1, − 2, − 3, …}]

1. [MATH: -\sqrt{3}]
2. [MATH: - 0.2]
3. [MATH: 0]
4. [MATH: -\sqrt{4}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-] is the set of all negative rational numbers.

  • [MATH: -\sqrt{3}] is negative but not a rational number, so it does not belong to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{red}\times]

  • [MATH: -0.2] is negative, and it is a rational number because it can be written as a ratio of two integers: [MATH: -0.2 = -\dfrac{1}{5}] Therefore, [MATH: -0.2] belongs to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

  • [MATH: 0] is a rational number but not negative, so it does not belong to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{red}\times]

  • [MATH: -\sqrt{4} =- 2], and it is a rational number because it can be written as a ratio of two integers: [MATH: -\sqrt 4 = -2 = -\dfrac{2}{1}] Therefore, [MATH: -\sqrt 4] belongs to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II and IV only."

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Some sets are so important that special symbols are used to represent them.

Content:
- The set [MATH: \mathbb{N}] represents the set of natural numbers. This set contains all the positive whole numbers:
[MATH: \Bbb{N} = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, ... \}]
It's essential to remember that the natural numbers do not contain zero! However, if we wish to refer to the set of natural numbers and zero, we use the symbol [MATH: \mathbb N_0{:}]
[MATH: \Bbb{N}_0 = \{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5,... \}]
- The set [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] represents the set of integers. This set contains the positive and negative whole numbers and zero.
[MATH: \Bbb{Z} = \left\{... , -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... \right\}]
The use of the letter "Z" comes from the German word "Zahlen," which means "numbers".
- The set [MATH: \mathbb{Q}] represents the set of rational numbers. This set contains all fractions that can be expressed as the ratio (or Quotient) of two integers.
- The set [MATH: \mathbb{R}] represents the set of real numbers. This set contains all possible rational and irrational numbers (such as [MATH: \pi, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \ldots]).
- The set [MATH: \mathbb C] represents the set of complex numbers. These consist of any number of the form [MATH: a+\textrm i b,] where [MATH: a,b\in\mathbb R.]

Content:
We can think of these special sets as being arranged in a hierarchy, as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a6ee882d08ea5e8bcbb01f43dfd9f07f]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Special Sets Containing a Given Element

Example Prompt:
Consider the following sets:
[MATH: \mathbb N, \quad \mathbb Z, \quad \mathbb Q, \quad \mathbb R, \quad \mathbb C]

To which of these sets does the number [MATH: 3.25] belong?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
[IMG: /graphics/0d72f30929eeba5e9f3763f164935f47]

Recall the following:

- [MATH: \mathbb{N}] represents the set of natural numbers.
- [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] represents the set of integers.
- [MATH: \mathbb{Q}] represents the set of rational numbers.
- [MATH: \mathbb{R}] represents the set of real numbers.
- [MATH: \mathbb C] represents the set of complex numbers.

With that in mind, we note the following:

- The number [MATH: 3.25] is not an integer, so it does not belong to [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] nor [MATH: \mathbb{N},] so we can write
[MATH: 3.25\notin\mathbb N, \qquad 3.25\notin\mathbb Z.]
- However, notice that [MATH: 3.25] can be written as the ratio of two integers as follows:
[MATH: 3.25=\dfrac{325}{100}]
Consequently, [MATH: 3.25] is a rational number, and we can write
[MATH: 3.25 \in \mathbb{Q}.]
- Every rational is a real and complex number. Consequently, [MATH: 3.25] belongs to both [MATH: \mathbb R] and [MATH: \mathbb{C},] and we can write
[MATH: 3.25 \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad 3.25 \in \mathbb{C}.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \mathbb Q, \mathbb R,] and [MATH: \mathbb C] only."

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Subscript and Superscript Notation With Special Sets

Content:
We can use subscripts and superscripts to limit the special sets to being only positive ("[MATH: +]" superscript), only negative ("[MATH: -]" superscript), and to include zero ("[MATH: 0]" subscript).

Content:
For example, [MATH: \mathbb{Z}^+] represents the positive integers, while [MATH: \mathbb{Z}^-] represents the negative integers:

Content:
[MATH: Z^{+}|= {1, 2, 3, …}; Z^{−}|= {− 1, − 2, − 3, …}]

Content:
These sets do not include [MATH: 0.] If we want to include [MATH: 0] too, then we can use a subscript [MATH: 0,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: Z_{0}^{+}|= {0, 1, 2, 3, …}; Z_{0}^{−}|= {0, − 1, − 2, − 3, …}]

Content:
A table describing all the special sets is given below.

Content:
| Symbol | Meaning |
| [MATH: \emptyset] | The empty set, [MATH: \{\}] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{N}] | The set of natural numbers, [MATH: \{1,2,3,...\}] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{N}_0] | The set of natural numbers and zero, [MATH: \{0,1,2,3,...\}] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Z}] | The set of integers, [MATH: \{0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,...\}] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Z}^+] | The set of positive integers, [MATH: \{1,2,3,...\}.] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Z}_0^+] | The set of positive integers and zero, [MATH: \{0,1,2,3,...\}] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Z}^-] | The set of negative integers, [MATH: \{-1,-2,-3,...\}] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Z}_0^-] | The set of negative integers and zero, [MATH: \{0,-1,-2,-3,...\}] |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Q}] | The set of rational numbers |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^+] | The set of positive rational numbers |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Q}_0^+] | The set of positive rational numbers and zero |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-] | The set of negative rational numbers |
| [MATH: \mathbb{Q}_0^-] | The set of negative rational numbers and zero |
| [MATH: \mathbb{R}] | The set of real numbers |
| [MATH: \mathbb{R}^+] | The set of positive real numbers |
| [MATH: \mathbb{R}_0^+] | The set of positive real numbers and zero |
| [MATH: \mathbb{R}^-] | The set of negative real numbers |
| [MATH: \mathbb{R}_0^-] | The set of negative real numbers and zero |

---

Item 7 — Example: Identifying Elements Belonging to Scripted Special Sets

Example Prompt:
Which of the numbers below belong to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-?]

1. [MATH: -\sqrt{3}]
2. [MATH: - 0.2]
3. [MATH: 0]
4. [MATH: -\sqrt{4}]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-] is the set of all negative rational numbers.

- [MATH: -\sqrt{3}] is negative but not a rational number, so it does not belong to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{red}\times]
- [MATH: -0.2] is negative, and it is a rational number because it can be written as a ratio of two integers:
[MATH: -0.2 = -\dfrac{1}{5}]
Therefore, [MATH: -0.2] belongs to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]
- [MATH: 0] is a rational number but not negative, so it does not belong to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{red}\times]
- [MATH: -\sqrt{4} =- 2], and it is a rational number because it can be written as a ratio of two integers:
[MATH: -\sqrt 4 = -2 = -\dfrac{2}{1}]
Therefore, [MATH: -\sqrt 4] belongs to [MATH: \mathbb{Q}^-. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II and IV only."
